extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in research integrity (researchers, editors, science journalists, and watchdogs)
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and summarizing retractions and expressions of concern in an academic journal, with attention to possible paper-mill links, publisher actions, and count/label accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate classification of notices (retraction vs expression of concern vs correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish retractions from expressions of concern and corrections when counting or reporting. The piece notes a database entry that marked an EoC or correction as a retraction and a publisher link that redirected incorrectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the publisher's notice and DOI before declaring an item retracted; errors in labeling can change counts and conclusions. When mistakes are found, correct reporting and add a correction note (as Retraction Watch did).

rubrics_metrics.name: Count retractions carefully and transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: Report an explicit, verifiable count of retractions (e.g., 'By our count ... has now retracted 39 papers') and be ready to revise if the status of items changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a clear method for counting (which notice types are included), check publisher pages, and publicly correct counts when new information arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of paper-mill involvement: fabricated images and mass patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for systemic signs such as fabricated or duplicated images across dozens or hundreds of papers; the article cites sleuths who found evidence that more than 400 articles generated by a suspected mill contained fabricated images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use image forensics and pattern analysis (as independent sleuths do) to flag likely paper-mill output; cluster size and repeated image manipulation are strong indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship concerns as a red flag (alt authorship/affiliation changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant or complete post-acceptance changes to authorship and affiliations (e.g., original submission names replaced by paying customers) suggest paper-mill activity or fraudulent submission practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track author/affiliation changes between submission and publication; unusual replacement of entire authorship lists should prompt investigation and possible authorship-concern notices or retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of independent sleuthing and post-publication peer review (e.g., PubPeer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent data sleuths and platforms like PubPeer play a central role in identifying problematic papers; the article credits sleuths including Elisabeth Bik and PubPeer flags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists and editors should consider community-posted evidence and sleuth analyses when investigating suspected misconduct; these sources can direct formal editorial inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher and journal response guided by ethics policies (COPE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal editors and publishers should base decisions (retraction, EoC, correction) on established publishing ethics and COPE guidelines, as demonstrated in the quoted retraction notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow COPE and publisher policies when deciding corrective actions; document reasons and link to the relevant guidelines in notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain the scholarly record with transparent retraction practice
rubrics_metrics.description: When retracting, keep the article online but digitally watermark it as 'Retracted' to preserve the record while indicating its status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retractions should be clearly labeled and remain accessible to maintain transparency; notices should explain the reason for retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume a single source for clustered problems (avoid overgeneralization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about attributing many retractions to 'one such mill' without firm evidence; the article records a correction after commenters noted diverse origins and that some retracted items were not flagged by the same sleuths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate provenance and cross-check geographic/authorship patterns before asserting that multiple problematic papers come from the same paper mill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize varied reasons for retraction (data integrity, authorship concerns, error admissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions in the covered journal were for multiple reasons: fabricated data/images, authorship concerns, and cases where authors admitted fundamental errors upon checking their data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting or evaluating retractions, list the explicit reason(s) given in the publisher's notice rather than assuming a single cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher responsiveness varies and affects outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Different publishers respond differently to critiques (example: Royal Society of Chemistry retracted dozens; Elsevier journals were said to be ignoring critiques), which affects how quickly and thoroughly problems are addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for publisher-specific practices and responsiveness when assessing the scale and remediation of problematic literature; compare across publishers rather than treating all equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public corrections and editorial transparency are essential
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting errors (in counts, characterizations, or links), issue public corrections and explain changes; Retraction Watch edited its headline/sentence and added a correction note after being alerted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain trust by publicly acknowledging and correcting mistakes in reporting; include correction timestamps and explain what changed.
